title: Sorting in .NET
sub: What Array.Sort promises, stability and its price, comparers, a ulong render key and sorting without comparisons
cards/0/title: What Array.Sort promises — and what it does not
cards/0/body:
In the lesson on common mistakes we saw that Array.Sort and List<T>.Sort are an introspective sort (List.Sort just sorts its internal array). Now for what that means in an interview. There are three guarantees:

1. O(n log n) in the worst case — on any input, even one crafted against quicksort. 10⁶ elements take about n·log₂ n ≈ 2·10⁷ comparisons; 10⁴ sprites take about 1.3·10⁵.
2. In place: no copy of the array, only O(log n) of recursion stack on top.
3. Unstable: elements with equal keys may come out in a different order from the one they went in.

The third one is sneaky. Ranges of 4 to 16 elements are finished with insertion sort, and insertion sort keeps equal elements in order. So a test on five units "shows" stability, while on a thousand the equal ones get shuffled: partitioning around the pivot moves them across the whole array. Never rely on the order of equal elements after Sort.
cards/0/deep:
How introsort works in .NET (ArraySortHelper in dotnet/runtime). The pivot is the median of three: first, middle and last. After partitioning, it recurses into the right part and handles the left part in the same loop. The depth limit is 2·(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1); once it runs out, heapsort finishes that range — hence the O(n log n) worst case and an O(log n) bound on the stack. Ranges of up to 16 elements (IntrosortSizeThreshold) go to insertion sort, while ranges of 2 and 3 elements get a fixed chain of "swap if greater". That chain no longer keeps equals in order: [(1, a), (1, b), (0, c)] comes out as (0, c), (1, b), (1, a).

Why not merge sort. Merge sort is stable and also O(n log n), but it needs a buffer of n elements. The library chose "in place" over stability. OrderBy is stable for a different reason: it sorts an array of indices and breaks ties between equal keys by comparing the indices themselves.

Floating point. For float[] and double[] without a comparer, .NET 5+ first gathers all NaNs at the front and sorts the rest with direct comparisons. The result matches CompareTo: NaN is less than any number.
cards/1/q: What is true about List<T>.Sort in .NET? Select all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: The worst case is O(n log n), even on a deliberately crafted input
cards/1/options/1: It makes no copy of the list: it sorts the internal array in place
cards/1/options/2: Elements with equal keys keep their original order
cards/1/options/3: If equal elements kept their order on 5 elements, they will on 10⁵ as well
cards/1/options/4: Sorting 10⁶ elements takes on the order of 2·10⁷ comparisons
cards/1/explain: Introsort switches to heapsort when quicksort recurses too deep, so there is no quadratic case. It works in place with an O(log n) stack on top. n·log₂ n for n = 10⁶ is about 2·10⁷. But the order of equals is not guaranteed: up to 16 elements insertion sort runs and equal elements usually stay put; on larger arrays partitioning shuffles them. A small test proves nothing here.
cards/2/title: When you need stability and how to get it
cards/2/body:
Stability matters when elements with equal keys already have a meaningful order: events with the same timestamp in arrival order (a replay must play back the same way), players with equal scores by who got there first, a table sorted by one column and then by another.

Option 1 — LINQ. OrderBy, ThenBy and their Descending versions are stable. The price is memory: the source is copied into a buffer, next to it go a key array and an index array, plus iterators and the resulting list. Fine for a sort while a level loads, not every frame.

Option 2 — remove equality. Append to the key something that tells any two elements apart: an arrival sequence number, a unique id. With no equal keys left, an unstable Sort has exactly one possible output — and no allocations.

The trap — two passes. "Sort by the second key, then by the first" only works with a stable sort: the second pass must keep the order the first pass built. List.Sort will destroy it.
cards/3/q: A leaderboard: by score descending, ties by name. Tests with five players pass; with 500 players the names among equal scores are scrambled. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/3/explain: The second Sort is unstable and need not keep the name order among equal scores. With five players insertion sort runs and the order of equals survives; with 500 it does not. The fix is one pass with a composite comparer: compare scores, and on a tie compare names. Or OrderByDescending(p => p.Score).ThenBy(p => p.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal) if allocations do not matter.
cards/4/title: Comparers: the contract and the cost of a call
cards/4/body:
Compare(a, b) < 0 means "a goes before b", 0 means "equal", > 0 means "a goes after". The sort trusts the comparer and needs it to keep a contract: Compare(a, a) == 0; the sign of Compare(a, b) is the opposite of Compare(b, a); if a goes before b and b before c, then a goes before c. Break it and you get a wrong order or the exception "IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results".

How people break it: a - b with overflow (from the lesson on mistakes); a < b ? -1 : 1 — it never returns 0, so an element is "greater than itself"; comparing float with < when NaN is around — every comparison with NaN is false. CompareTo gets all of this right. For descending order, swap the arguments: b.CompareTo(a); negating with -x breaks if the comparer returned int.MinValue.

Cost. Without a comparer, Array.Sort compares numbers directly: in .NET 5+ it is a plain < inside the sort code, in Unity (Mono and IL2CPP) a direct CompareTo call, again with no delegate. With a lambda, every comparison is an indirect delegate call that the JIT generally does not inline: ~n·log₂ n calls, 2·10⁷ for a million elements. And a lambda that captures a local also creates a closure and a new delegate on every call of the method — garbage for the GC. Hence the trick: if the key can be reduced to a number, sort numbers.
cards/4/deep:
Under the hood. In dotnet/runtime a sort without a comparer (or with Comparer<T>.Default) goes through GenericArraySortHelper<T>: for int, long, ulong, float, double and other primitives the comparison is the built-in operator; for other T : IComparable<T> it is a direct CompareTo call. If you pass your own IComparer<T>, its Compare method is turned into a Comparison<T> delegate — a new object per Sort call and an indirect call per comparison.

Lambda allocations. A lambda that captures nothing is cached by the compiler, so repeated Sort calls produce no garbage. A lambda that captures a local (say, the player position to compare distances) creates a closure and a delegate on every call of the method. In hot code, precompute the distances into a key array — faster and capture-free.

Shuffling with a "random comparer" — Sort((a, b) => rnd.Next(-1, 2)) — breaks the contract: the result is biased and the sort is allowed to throw. A fair shuffle is Fisher–Yates from the binary search unit.
cards/5/body:
A pair of arrays. Array.Sort(keys, items) sorts keys and applies the same moves to items. The keys are numbers, so comparisons are direct, no delegate; the data rides along, no tuples or comparers needed. The typical case is distances in a float[] and enemy indices in an int[].

Part of an array. The overloads Array.Sort(array, index, length) and Array.Sort(keys, items, index, length) sort only a range. That matters for pooled buffers: the array is 1024 long but only count elements are filled — sorting the whole array drags garbage from the tail to the front.

Span. .NET 5+ has MemoryExtensions.Sort: span.Sort(), span.Sort(comparison) and keys.Sort(items) for two Spans — handy for a stackalloc buffer or a slice of an array. Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have these methods: AsSpan is there, but there is no Sort on the result. Sort the array with an index and a length instead.

NativeArray. In the com.unity.collections package, NativeArray<T> has Sort() for T : unmanaged, IComparable<T> and an overload taking your own comparer as a struct IComparer<T>. A struct is not a delegate: Burst knows its type at compile time, so the Compare call is direct and usually inlined.
cards/6/q: Unity, every frame: 10⁴ enemies in a pooled buffer (count filled), you need them ordered by distance to the player, with no GC garbage. What do you pick?
cards/6/options/0: Distances in float[], indices in int[]: Array.Sort(dist, idx, 0, count)
cards/6/explain: The key is computed once per enemy rather than twice per comparison; float comparison is direct, no delegate; only the filled part is sorted; no new objects — dist and idx live in fields and are reused.
cards/6/wrong/1: OrderBy is stable, but every frame it creates a buffer, a key array, an index array and the result array — garbage for the Boehm GC 60 times a second.
cards/6/wrong/2: The lambda captures player — a closure and a delegate on every call of the method. The distance is computed in every comparison, about 2·n·log₂ n times instead of n. And the whole buffer gets sorted, stale tail past count included.
cards/6/wrong/3: In Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) Span has no Sort method — that is .NET 5+. Besides, it is unclear what comparing enemies "by default" would mean: you need a separate key anyway.
cards/7/title: Unity: transparents by depth, sprites by layer — a key in a ulong
cards/7/body:
What Unity does itself. Transparent objects are drawn back to front by the distance from the camera to the object's center — otherwise a near semi-transparent object gets painted over by a far one. Opaque ones go roughly front to back: near objects write depth first, and the depth test rejects hidden pixels before the shader runs — less overdraw. In SRP these are the flags SortingCriteria.CommonTransparent (with BackToFront) and CommonOpaque (with QuantizedFrontToBack). For 2D objects (sprites, tiles), Sorting Layer and Order in Layer come first, then the material's render queue, and only then distance to the camera; for a top-down view people set Transparency Sort Mode = Custom Axis (0, 1, 0) — sorting by Y.

When you sort yourself — your own instancing (Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced), particles of your own system, bullets in a bullet hell — a three-field comparer means branches and a delegate call per comparison. The engine trick: pack all keys into one number so that comparing numbers matches comparing tuples. The high bits hold the main key: 63–48 — layer, 47–32 — order in layer, 31–0 — depth.

Depth as bits. For a float ≥ 0, the IEEE-754 bit pattern read as a uint grows with the value — order is preserved. Back to front means far ones first: invert the bits, ~d. Order in Layer in Unity ranges from −32768 to 32767; adding 32768 makes it unsigned, 0..65535. Then Array.Sort(keys, ids, 0, count) on ulong: direct comparison.
cards/7/deep:
Negative floats. If the key can be negative (a Y coordinate for top-to-bottom sorting), the bits of negative numbers run the other way. The standard transform: for non-negative values flip the sign bit, for negative ones flip all bits: u = (bits & 0x80000000) != 0 ? ~bits : bits | 0x80000000. The result is a uint whose order matches the order of the numbers.

Quantization. Opaque objects do not need all 32 bits of depth: objects at similar depth barely overlap anyway. Depth is squeezed into 10–16 bits, and the freed bits go to a material or shader id — objects sharing a material end up next to each other, with fewer GPU state changes. That is what Quantized means in QuantizedFrontToBack.

Why transparents "flicker". Sorting is per object, not per pixel: for two intersecting transparent meshes, the center of one is sometimes nearer and sometimes farther, and the order jumps as the camera moves. The fixes are splitting the mesh, a depth prepass, or order-independent transparency techniques — sorting cannot fix it.
cards/8/q: A key for opaque objects: layer first, then the material id (fewer state changes), then depth — near ones first. Fill in the blanks.
cards/8/explain: The layer takes the top 16 bits: shift by 48. The material takes the next 16 bits, 47–32. Depth goes into the low 32 bits as is: for a float ≥ 0 the bits grow with the value, so a smaller key is nearer. Transparents used ~d because there far ones go first. The raw depth cannot go here: a float cannot be shifted or OR-ed with a ulong.
cards/9/title: When you need no comparisons: counting and radix sort
cards/9/body:
Any comparison sort needs at least log₂ n! ≈ n·log₂ n comparisons in the worst case: there are n! possible orders, and each comparison rules out at most half of them. The only way around the bound is not to compare.

Counting sort. The keys are integers in a small range [0, k): levels 0..99, an age, a layer number. Count how often each key occurs, use prefix sums to find where each key starts, and place the elements — left to right, so the sort is stable. Time O(n + k), memory O(n + k). In the heaps unit the same trick — buckets by frequency — will give top-K in O(n).

Radix sort (LSD). The key is wide — a uint, a ulong. Counting-sort by the lowest byte, then by the next one, up to the highest: 256 buckets, 4 passes for a uint, 8 for a ulong. It works because of stability: the pass on byte j does not disturb the order the lower bytes established among elements with an equal byte j. Time O(w·(n + 256)), where w is the number of bytes, plus a buffer of n.

When it pays off: n from tens of thousands, keys are fixed-width integers (like the key from the previous card). When it does not: small n — the overhead of 256 buckets outweighs the gain; keys that are compared in a complex way (culture-aware strings).
cards/9/deep:
Data alongside the key. In real code the object id travels with the key: either a second array permuted with the same indices, or the id in the low bits of the key itself if there is room (24 bits of depth + an 8-bit id and so on).

Skipping passes. If every element lands in one bucket (all share a layer, so the high bytes are equal), the pass changes nothing: count shows this before placing, and the pass can be skipped.

Nearly sorted data. Between consecutive frames, the depth order of particles barely changes. Insertion sort runs in O(n + inversions): on a nearly ordered array that is almost O(n) — faster than both radix sort and introsort. That is why particles are often re-sorted with insertion sort, starting from last frame's order.

Counting without placing. If the key is the value itself (an array of 0, 1, 2 with no attached data), there is nothing to place: count, then write the values out in order. That is the next card.
cards/10/body:
The problem. An array of 0s, 1s and 2s (red, white, blue). Sort it in place without the library sort. Counting takes two passes: count each value, then rewrite the array. The interviewer will ask: can you do it in one pass?

Three pointers (the Dutch national flag problem). The array splits into four zones: [0, lo) — zeros, [lo, mid) — ones, [mid, hi] — not looked at yet, (hi, n − 1] — twos. Each step shrinks the unknown zone by one:

a[mid] == 0 — swap with a[lo]: a zero goes there, and a one comes back to mid (or the zero itself if lo == mid); advance both.
a[mid] == 1 — already in place, mid++.
a[mid] == 2 — swap with a[hi], hi--. Do not move mid: the element that came from hi has not been seen yet.

Stop when mid > hi: the unknown zone is empty. O(n), one pass, O(1) memory. In a game — partition an entity array in place into three groups: opaque, alpha-tested and transparent; alive, stunned, dead. The rig runs it next.
cards/11/task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0]. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the zones and pointers on screen.
cards/11/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Swap with nums[5]; hi = 4, mid stays 1
cards/11/goal/asks/0/q: lo = 0, mid = 1, hi = 5, nums[1] = 2. What does the code do?
cards/11/goal/asks/0/explain: The 2 goes to the twos: swap with nums[5], hi = 4. But mid stays: a 0 came from hi, and nobody has looked at it yet. With mid++ in this branch the zero would stay behind mid, among the ones, and the array would not end up sorted: on [1, 2, 0] that gives [1, 0, 2]. Swapping with lo has no such problem — what comes to mid from there is a 1 that was already checked.
cards/11/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: 0 — a zero swaps with a zero
cards/11/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: 2 — it will be sent to hi later
cards/11/goal/asks/1/q: nums = [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2], lo = 1, mid = 2, nums[2] = 0 — swap with nums[lo]. What lands at mid?
cards/11/goal/asks/1/explain: The zone [lo, mid) holds ones, so nums[lo] = 1. After the swap the zero joins the zeros and the one moves to the end of the ones zone, at mid. That is why mid moves together with lo in this branch: the element that arrived is already checked. A 2 can never come from lo — every 2 found so far sits past hi.
cards/12/q: Sort Colors in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: only 0, 1 and 2? In place? Are two passes allowed?
cards/12/items/1: Name the simple options: counting in two passes, O(n), or Array.Sort in O(n log n)
cards/12/items/2: The one-pass idea: four zones and the pointers lo, mid, hi
cards/12/items/3: Code it, stating the zone invariant; mid does not move after a swap with hi
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory, one pass
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: empty array, one element, all equal, no ones at all
cards/12/explain: First the conditions and the simple counting solution — it is already O(n), and you should say so. Then what the problem is really about: the zone invariant and its one subtlety, mid after a swap with hi. The example [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] exercises both swap branches.
